summary:
Dancing with the SARs, by team AstroRatas, is an interactive Streamlit web app that uses NISAR L-band radar to reveal possible forest-cover changes in Chocó, Colombia, where illegal mining drives deforestation and persistent clouds block optical satellites. Users explore a satellite map and click study zones (Baudocito, San Isidro in Río Quito, Pie de Pató and Nuquí) to see NISAR GCOV animations, multitemporal analysis panels, radar-change maps and a breakdown of hectares with possible change. Behind the app is a reproducible Python pipeline that streams only the area of interest from NISAR L2 GCOV products in NASA Earthdata Cloud, filters speckle, compares HH and HV backscatter across dates, flags persistent HV decreases (HV is most sensitive to vegetation volume) as change candidates, separates ambiguous changes near water or radar shadow, and groups them into patches. A before/after section also shows natural changes, such as soil moisture after rain, so users learn to tell them apart from human impact.

NISAR sees through clouds every 12 days with free data, turning a hard-to-monitor region into one that can be watched frequently. Our results are candidates to prioritize field verification, not confirmed deforestation.
details:
Dancing with the SARs is an interactive web application that turns NISAR radar data into an accessible picture of where the forest of Chocó, Colombia, may be changing. Chocó is one of the rainiest and cloudiest regions on Earth and a hotspot of illegal gold mining, so optical satellites rarely provide a clear view. NISAR's L-band radar penetrates clouds and interacts with the forest canopy, which makes it well suited to this problem.

In the app, users explore a satellite basemap of Chocó and click on study zones (Baudocito, San Isidro in Río Quito, Pie de Pató and Nuquí). Each zone opens a report with a NISAR GCOV animation, a multitemporal analysis panel, radar-change maps and an interactive bar showing how many hectares fall into each change class. An "Other Data Applications" section uses a before/after slider in RGB false color (R=HH, G=HV, B=HV/HH) to show natural changes, such as higher surface moisture after rain, so users can learn to tell them apart from human impact.

Behind the app is a reproducible Python pipeline:

1. Search: earthaccess queries NASA's catalog for NISAR L2 GCOV products over each zone between June and October 2026. To avoid false changes, the pipeline keeps a single orbit track, frame and processing version, and selects six dates spread evenly in time.

2. Streaming subset: GDAL reads only a 10 x 10 km window directly from the HDF5 files in NASA Earthdata Cloud (/vsicurl/ with HTTP range requests) and resamples HH and HV to a common 20 m UTM grid, so full scenes never need to be downloaded.

3. Speckle reduction: an adaptive Lee filter (3x3 window) is applied and backscatter is converted to decibels.

4. Change detection: early (first two dates) and late (last two dates) composites are compared. A pixel becomes a "persistent HV decrease" candidate when HV drops at least 2 dB and both late dates stay at least 1.5 dB below the baseline. HV (cross-polarization) is the channel most sensitive to vegetation volume, so its loss is a proxy for canopy disturbance. A linear HV trend (dB/month) is also computed across all six dates.

5. Ambiguity control: candidates within about 40 m of very dark surfaces (water or radar shadow) are labeled "radiometrically ambiguous" instead of being counted as possible forest loss.

6. Patch analysis: candidates are grouped into 8-connected patches; their area, location and distance to ambiguous pixels are exported as CSV, GeoJSON and GeoTIFF, together with maps, animations and a summary report.

Results so far: San Isidro (Río Quito) shows 635.20 ha of change candidates (6.20% of the area), with the most continuous detections along the river corridor and a largest patch of 3.68 ha. Pie de Pató shows 275.52 ha (2.73%) and Nuquí 98.28 ha (0.97%), mostly as isolated pixels; no patch reaches 0.5 ha in either zone.

The approach works regardless of cloud cover, uses free NASA data, runs on an ordinary laptop, and can be applied to a new zone by editing a single configuration file. It is intended for environmental authorities, community councils, NGOs and journalists who must decide where to send limited field teams. Instead of issuing verdicts, it points to where to look first, and it helps the public understand what radar images can and cannot show.

The name and design play with the idea that Earth's surface is in a constant "dance" of change. Analysis windows styled as radar terminals, map-first exploration and the before/after slider make radar data approachable for non-specialists. We also separate "ambiguous" changes from candidates explicitly, so the app shows its own uncertainty instead of hiding it.

We considered speckle noise; radar geometry effects (layover and shadow) in hilly terrain; rivers and sea surfaces, whose backscatter changes with wind and waves; rain and soil moisture; and consistency of track, frame and processing version. Zones observed from different orbit tracks, such as Nuquí, are not compared directly with the others. Because results have not yet been validated with independent forest data, every output states that they are candidate changes, not confirmed deforestation, to be verified in the field or with other sources.

We used Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, Matplotlib, Pillow, earthaccess), GDAL 3.13 with its HDF5 driver, Pixi for reproducible environments, NASA Earthdata Login and ASF Vertex for data access, Streamlit, Folium and streamlit-folium for the web app, Esri World Imagery as basemap, and GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud for deployment. Development was done on personal computers running Linux.

We used generative AI assistants (such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) as support tools for programming and writing: setting up the processing environment, debugging, adapting the pipeline to new zones, creating visualization scripts, and drafting and translating texts and reports. The team ran all code on real NISAR data, checked the outputs, and remained responsible for the methodological decisions and the interpretation of results.
